translations.title: The Tree of Knowledge
translations.text:
A window onto the world

For my hotel at night a sky rises
from the estuary slowly. It burns

a bog of stars and this solitary square
remains and in

silence.
Without the sleepless lights of the tram,
without its yellow

fruit and without its roar
the steep streets fall asleep,
they

empty of children, and the shops
and the bars begin to close.
It is

the hill is gentle and the greens are
a ruined estate, some palms,

a sad and secure colonial air,
witnesses that the Tagus reaches the
sea
and black ships with light bulbs reach the port.
Its siren
is hoarse

like smoke!
Beautiful animals of the night,
funeral carriages

on the water!
Old cities where there is always someone
leaning out at the
balcony and at the windows.
If I could be at that height,

I would look in silence and last forever:
all the blue, the river and the
memory.
This street descends there where I cannot reach
to see, my hotel,

final place where I look at myself
and another in my place leaves my name in a
name of
another city and another river.

From “The Traditions,” 1991
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Andrés Trapiello. The source title is rendered literally; irregular syntax and line breaks are retained.

translations.title: I Want to Go with the One I Love...
translations.text:
Memory of Marie A.

1
On that blue-moon day in September
in silence beneath a
young plum tree
I held my pale, quiet love
in my arms

like a blessed dream.
And above us in the beautiful
summer sky
there was a cloud, which I watched for a long time;
it was very white
and terribly high
and when I looked up again, it
was no longer there.

2
Since that day many, many moons
have dived in
silence and passed.
The plum trees will have been uprooted
and if you
ask me, What became of that love?
then I answer you: I cannot
remember,
but even so, it is true, I know what you mean.
Although
I truly do not remember her face,
now I know only that then
I kissed her.

3
And I would have forgotten the kiss long ago
if that cloud had not
been there;
that I remember and always will
remember,
it was very white and came from above.
Perhaps the
plum trees still blossom
and that woman already has seven children,

but that cloud blossomed only for a few minutes
and when I looked
up it was vanishing in the wind.

Version by Jesús Munárriz and Jenaro Talens
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Bertolt Brecht. The supplied translator credit is retained and the numbered stanza structure preserved.

translations.title: After the Slaughterhouse...
translations.text:
After the slaughterhouse

Turning the corner, there was
a bar

where I sat and watched the sun fall

through the window,

a window looking onto a lot

full of tall, dry weeds.


I never took a shower with the boys
at the factory
after work

so I smelled of sweat and
blood

the smell of sweat diminished after
a while

but the blood-smell began to strike hard
and gain strength.


I smoked cigarettes and drank beer
until I felt well enough
to get on the bus

with the souls of all those dead animals
that traveled with me

the heads turned discreetly
the women stood up and moved away
from me.


when I got off the bus
I only had to go down one block
and climb a staircase to reach
my room where I would turn on the radio
and light a cigarette
and no one would be bothered by me.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The spare lowercase presentation and stanza spacing are retained.

translations.title: It Is the Man You Have Never Seen Who...
translations.text:
it is the man you have never seen who

keeps you alert,
the one who is to come
one day.


he is not in the streets or
in the buildings or in the
stadiums,
or if he is there
I have somehow overlooked him.


he is not one of our presidents
or statesmen or actors.


I wonder if he is there.


beneath the streets
I pass pharmacies and hospitals and
theaters and cafés
and wonder if he is there.


I have looked for almost half a century
and he has not been seen.


a living man, truly alive,
say when he lowers his hand
to light a cigarette
you see his eyes
like the eyes of a tiger staring
as it passes in the wind.


but when the hands lower
it is always the
other eyes
that are there
always always.


and soon it will be too late for me
and I will have lived a life
with pharmacies, cats, sheets, saliva,
newspapers, women, doors and assorted things,

but nowhere
a living man.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Lowercase form, repetitions, and lineation are preserved.

translations.title: Love and Courage
translations.text:
The one I liked was the one where Cagney
fought in the ring
with his fists alone
so he could win money
for his brother to have
music lessons
the brother wanted to be
a classical pianist
they had told him he had
great talent.


But the two of them came from the
poor neighborhood, and
Cagney had to climb into the ring
again and again
to get money and help his
talented brother
become a pianist.


Cagney even loses his girl
and the film ends with the brother
making it
(at Carnegie Hall, if I remember correctly)
and Cagney
beaten to a pulp and blind
at his little newsstand
listening on the radio
to his brother’s concert
and, of course, the girl is at the concert
admiring him, her eyes wide
while Cagney rests his hands on
a little heater
alone in the cold
listens to the radio
while his brother plays the piano


Cagney
knows nothing about music
and
hearing the final applause
thinks that
all the blows they gave him
were worth it.-
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The film reference, parenthetical aside, and lineation are retained; “Carnagie” is transparently corrected to Carnegie.

translations.title: This Woman Thinks She’s a Panther...
translations.text:
This woman thinks she’s a panther
and sometimes when we make love
she growls and spits
and her hair falls
and she looks through the strands
and shows her fangs
but I kiss her and continue making love.

Have you ever kissed a panther woman?


Have you seen a panther woman enjoying
the act of love?
You have not loved, friend.

You with your little dyed blondes,
you with your squirrels and little squirrels
your elephants and sheep
you should sleep with a panther.

You would never again want
squirrels, elephants, sheep, foxes,

wolves,
nothing but the panther woman,
the female panther pacing through your room,
the female panther pacing through your soul;
all other love songs are lies
when that soft black skin moves against you
and the sky falls across your back,
the female panther is the dream come true
and there is no return
or desire to return;
skin against you,
the search has ended
when your cock moves against the edge of Nirvana
and you are held in the eyes of a panther.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The erotic language, direct address, repetitions, and lineation are retained.

translations.title: Out of the Arms of One Love
translations.text:
out of the arms of one love
and already in the arms of another.


I have escaped dying on the cross
for a lady who smokes marijuana
writes songs and stories,
and is much kinder than the last one,
much much kinder,
and her sex is as good or better.


it is not pleasant to be put on the cross and left there,
more pleasant to forget a love that did not
fulfill
like every love
finally
does not last…


more pleasant to make love
on the beach in Del Mar
in room 42 and afterward
sitting on the bed
drinking good wine, talking and touching,
smoking.


listening to the waves…


I have died many times
believing and hoping, hoping
in a room
staring at a holed ceiling
waiting for the call, a letter, a little knock, a sound…


turning wild inside
while she danced with strangers in nightclubs…


out of the arms of one love
and already in the arms of another
it is not pleasant to die on the cross,
more pleasant to hear your name whispered in
the darkness.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Repetition, ellipses, explicit language, and stanza spacing are preserved.

translations.title: People Are Exhausted, Unhappy and Frustrated, People Are...
translations.text:
People are exhausted, unhappy and frustrated, people are
bitter and vengeful, people are deceived and afraid,
people are angry and mediocre
and I drive among them on the freeway and they
project what has been left of them
in the way they drive.

Some more hateful, some more disguised
than others.

Some do not like being passed, and try
to keep others from doing it.

Some try to block lane changes.

Some hate newer, more expensive cars.

Others in those cars hate older cars.

The freeway is a circus of
tiny and cheap emotions, it is
humanity in motion, most of it
coming from a place that
hates
and going to another place that hates
even more.

The freeways teach us what
we have become and
many of the crashes and deaths are the collision
between incomplete beings, between pitiful
and deranged lives.

When I drive on the freeways I see the soul of
my city and it is ugly, ugly, ugly: the living have
strangled
its heart.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The repeated “people,” freeway imagery, and lineation are preserved.

translations.title: There’s a Bluebird in My Heart That...
translations.text:
There’s a bluebird in my heart that
wants to get out
but I am hard on him,
I tell him stay in there, I am not going
to let anyone
see you.

There’s a bluebird in my heart that
wants to get out
but I pour whisky over him and inhale
cigarette smoke,
and the whores and the bartenders
and the grocery clerks
never realize
that he is in there.

There’s a bluebird in my heart that
wants to get out
but I am hard on him,
I tell him stay down there, do you want
to make a mess of me?

Do you want
my work?

Do you want my book sales to sink
in Europe?

There’s a bluebird in my heart
that wants to get out
but I am too clever, I only let him out
sometimes at night
when everybody sleeps.

I tell him I know you’re there,
don’t get
sad.

Then I put him back,
and he sings a little
in there, I have not let him
die completely
and we sleep together
like this
with our
secret pact
and it is tender enough
to make a man cry, but I do not
cry,
do you?
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The recurring bluebird refrain, colloquial tone, and lineation are retained.

translations.title: No One Can Save You but...
translations.text:
No one can save you but
yourself.

you will see yourself again and again
in situations
almost impossible.

they will try again and again
through subterfuge, deception or
by force
to make you give up, surrender and/or die slowly
inside.

No one can save you but
yourself
and it will be very easy to faint,
very easy,
but do not faint, no, no
just look at them.

listen to them.

Do you want to be like that?

A faceless, mindless
heartless being?

Do you want to experience
death before death?

No one can save you but
yourself
and you deserve to save yourself.

It is not an easy war to win
but if anything is worth winning,
it is this.

Think about it.

Think about saving yourself.
your spiritual part.
the part of your guts.
your magical and drunken part.
save it.

Do not join the spiritually dead.

Stay
in good humor and style
and in the end,
if necessary,
bet your life in the thick of the fight,
to hell with the odds, to hell with
the price.

No one can save you but
yourself.

Do it! Save yourself!

then you will know exactly
what I am talking about.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Repeated imperatives, direct address, and stanza breaks are preserved.

translations.title: I Locked the Car Door...
translations.text:
I locked the car door
and when I looked up I saw this guy
walking toward me
he looked like Peter, my old friend
but he wasn’t Peter
he was a gaunt man
in jeans and a blue work shirt
and he said to me:

“hey, my wife and I
need something to eat,
we’re starving”

I looked behind him
and there she was,
his wife
who looked at me with eyes
on the verge of tears.

I gave him a five-dollar bill.

“I love you, man!” he shouted,
“I won’t spend it on booze.”

“Why not?” I answered,
“That’s what I would do…”

I walked away to enter a building
settled a few matters
came out
returned to the car
as always
thinking
whether I had done the right thing
or whether I had been conned.


while driving
I remembered my years
of misery
hungry beyond any remedy
I never asked anyone
for a cent.


that night, after a few drinks,
I explained to the woman I lived with
how much money I gave to bums
but how I
in the darkest times
of hunger in my life
refused to ask anyone for anything.


“the thing is, you weren’t even
good at that,” she said.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Dialogue, lowercase presentation, and lineation are preserved.

translations.title: They Are Everywhere
translations.text:
The tragedy-sniffers are
everywhere
they get up in the morning
and start finding things
wrong.

And they plunge
into rage,
a rage that lasts until
they go to bed,
and even there
they writhe in their
insomnia,
unable to remove
from their minds
the small obstacles
they have found.

They feel opposed,
it is a conspiracy.

And because they are constantly
furious they feel that
they are always
right.

You see them in traffic
honking like savages
at the slightest infraction,
cursing,
scattering their
insults.

You feel them
in bank lines,
in supermarkets,
in cinemas
pressing
against your back
treading on your heels
impatient for
a fury.

They are everywhere
and in
everything,
those souls
violently
unhappy.

In truth they are frightened,
as always they want to
be right
whipping
without cease…
it is an evil
a disease of
that race.

The first of them
I saw was
my father
and since then
I have seen a thousand fathers
wasting their lives
in hatred,
throwing their lives
into the blind well
and screaming
like madmen.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The mixed regional forms and harsh repetitive cadence are rendered in direct English.

translations.title: The Best and the Worst
translations.text:
Hospitals and prisons
are the worst
asylums
are the worst
attics
are the worst
noisy little hotels
are the worst
poetry readings
rock concerts
for the benefit of the disabled
are the worst
funerals
weddings
are the worst
parades
skating rinks
sexual orgies
are the worst
midnight
3 in the morning
5:45 in the afternoon
are the worst.

Falling from the sky
firing squads
that is the best
thinking of India
watching popcorn stands
seeing the bull take the matador
that is the best
light bulbs in boxes
an old dog digging
peanuts in a paper bag
that is the best
spraying cockroaches
a pair of clean socks
natural courage defeating natural talent
that is the best
standing before firing squads
throwing crumbs to gulls
slicing tomatoes
that is the best
carpets burned with cigarettes
cracks in sidewalks
waitresses still sane
that is the best
my dead hands
my dead heart
silence
adagio of rocks
the world in flames
that is the best
for me.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The deliberately repetitive catalog and lineation are preserved.

translations.title: Drug
translations.text:
Sitting in a dark bedroom with 3 drug-addicted
women.

There are brown paper bags with trash
everywhere.

It is one-thirty in the afternoon.

They talk about asylums,
about hospitals,
they are waiting for a dose
none of them works.

Everything is welfare and food stamps and
California Medical Center.

Men are objects used
to get the dose.

It is one-thirty in the afternoon
outside small plants are growing
their children are still at school.

They smoke cigarettes
and bored, sip beer
tequila
that I have bought.

I am sitting with them
and waiting for my dose:
I am a poetry addict.

Ezra was dragged through the streets
in a wooden cage.

Blake believed in God.

Villon was a thief.

Lorca sucked cocks.

T. S. Eliot worked as a teller at a window,
most poets are swans,
they are herons.

I am sitting with 3 drug-addicted women
at one-thirty in the afternoon.

The smoke is an ascending piss.

I wait.

Death is the Jumbo of nothingness.

One of the women says she likes
my yellow shirt.

I believe in natural violence.

That was part of it.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Explicit language, named poets, and lineation are retained.

translations.title: You Haven’t Lived...
translations.text:
You haven’t lived
until you have been in a
cheap boardinghouse
with nothing but one
bulb
and 56 men
crammed
in cots
and everyone
snoring at once
and some of those
snores
so
deep and
so crude and
incredible…
dark
guttural
inhuman
gasping
from hell itself.

It seems as if
your head were splitting
between those
sounds
of death.

And the
smells mingling:
dirty and
stiff socks and
underwear
with urine and
excrement
and above it all an air that
circulates slowly
very much like
that which comes from
uncovered garbage cans.

Those
bodies
in the darkness
fat
and thin
and hunched
some
without legs
without arms
others
without brains
and worst of
all: the total
absence of
hope
envelops them
covers them
completely.

It cannot be
borne.

You get up
go out
walk through
the streets
go up and down
sidewalks
pass buildings
turn the
corner
and go back up
the same street
thinking
all those men
were children
once
what
happened to them?

and what happened to
me?

it is dark
and cold
out
there.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The sensory catalog, fragmented syntax, and line breaks are preserved.

translations.title: Warm Buttocks
translations.text:
this Friday night
the Mexican girls at the Catholic carnival
look very good
their husbands are in the bars
and the Mexican girls look young
hooked nose with tremendous eyes,
warm buttocks in tight jeans
they have been grabbed somehow,
their husbands tired of those hot asses
and the Mexican girls walk with their children,
there is real sadness in their tremendous eyes
as if they remembered nights when their handsome men
told them so many beautiful things
beautiful things they will never hear again,
and under the moon and in the flashes of
carnival lights
I see it all and stand silent and feel sorry for them.

they see me watching
the old goat is looking at us
he is looking into our eyes;
they smile at each other, talk, leave together,
laugh, look at me over their shoulders.

I walk toward a booth
put a dime on number eleven and win a cake
of chocolate with 13 colored cherries on the
top

enough and more for an ex-Catholic
and an admirer of the hot and young and
no longer used
afflicted asses of the Mexican girls.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Sexualized imagery, colloquial voice, and lineation are retained.

translations.title: If We Consider
translations.text:
If we consider what can be seen:

engines that drive us crazy,
lovers who end by hating each other,
that fish in the market
staring back as it enters our
minds,

rotting flowers, flies caught in webs,
riots, roars of caged lions,
clowns in love with bills,
nations moving people like chess pawns,
thieves in daylight with wonderful
wives and wines at night,

overcrowded prisons,
the cliché of the unemployed,
dying grass, insignificant fires,
men old enough to love the
grave.

These and other things
show that life turns on a rotten axle.

But they have left us a little music
and a poster pinned in the corner
a glass of whisky, a blue tie
a thin volume of Rimbaud’s poems,
a horse running as if the devil were
twisting its tail
over the blue grass and the shouting
and then, again, love
like a car turning the corner
on time,
the city waiting
the wine and the Flowers
the water running through the lake
and summer and winter and summer and summer
and winter again.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The accumulating images, repetitions, and line breaks are preserved.

translations.title: Beer
translations.text:
I don’t know how many bottles of beer
I drank while waiting for things to
improve.

I don’t know how much wine, whisky
and beer,
mostly beer
I drank after
breaking up with a woman
waiting for the telephone to ring
waiting for the sound of footsteps,
and the telephone doesn’t ring
until much later
and the footsteps don’t come
until much later.

When my stomach comes out
through my mouth,
they arrive fresh as spring flowers:


-“What the fuck did you do?
It will be three days before you can fuck me”

A female lasts longer
lives seven and a half years longer
than the male, and drinks very little beer
because she knows it is bad for her
figure.

While we go crazy
they are out
dancing and laughing
with fun boys.


Well, there is beer
bags and bags of empty beer bottles
and when you lift one
it bottoms out
and the bottles fall
rolling
clinking
spilling wet gray ash
and old beer
or the bags fall at 4
in the morning
making the only sound in your life.


Beer
rivers and seas of beer
beer, beer, beer.

The radio plays love songs
while the telephone remains silent
and the walls loom
and beer is all there is.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The repeated “beer,” conversational profanity, and stanza layout are retained.

translations.title: My Pal
translations.text:
To be a 21-year-old boy in New Orleans I wasn’t
worth much: I had a little room that smelled of
urine and death
but I wanted to be there, and there were
two adorable girls at the end of the hall who
kept banging on my door and shouting. “Get up!
There are good things out there!”

“Get lost,” I told them, but that only
encouraged them more, they left notes under the door and
taped flowers to the
door knob.

I was steeped in cheap wine and green beer and
madness…

I met the old guy in the room
next door, somehow I felt as old as
he was; his feet and ankles were swollen and he couldn’t
tie his shoes.

Every day around one in the afternoon we went out for a walk
together and it was a very
slow walk: every step was painful for him.

When we approached the curb, I helped him
up and down
holding him by the elbow
and the back of his
belt, we managed it.

I liked him: he never questioned me
about what I did or did not do.

He should have been my father, and what I liked most
was what he said again and
again: “Nothing is worth
it.”

He was a
wise
man
those young girls should
have left him
the notes and
the flowers.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Dialogue, ellipsis, and deliberately plain lineation are preserved; minor Spanish accent errors are normalized in English.

translations.title: Betting on the Muse
translations.text:
Jimmy Foxx died of alcoholism
in a miserable hotel room.

Beau Jack ended up shining
shoes,
just when he was beginning.

There are dozens, hundreds,
more, perhaps a thousand more.

To be an aging athlete
is one of the cruelest
fates,
to be replaced by others,
no longer hearing the
acclaim and the experts, no longer being
recognized,
being only an old man
like any other
old man.

Almost enough not to believe
yourself,
you look through the scrapbook
with its yellowing
pages. And there you are,
smiling;
there you are,
victorious;
there you are,
young.

The crowd has other
heroes.

The crowd never
dies,
never grows old
but the crowd often
forgets
now the telephone
doesn’t ring,
the girls have
gone,
the party
is over.

That is why I chose
to be a
writer.

If you are worth a
damn thing
you can continue with
your fooling around
until the last minute
of the last
day.

You can keep
improving instead
of getting worse,
you can keep
slamming them against the
wall.

Through the darkness, the war,
with good or bad
luck
you can keep hitting them,
with the dazzling lightning
of the
word,
knocking life down in life,
and death too late to
truly win
against
you.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Sports names, repeated “crowd,” and the poem’s lineation are retained; capitalization is normalized for the proper names.
